description_full: The Marzetti Company engages in manufacturing and marketing of specialty food products for the retail and foodservice channels in the United States. It operates in two segments, Retail and Foodservice. The Retail segment offers frozen garlic bread under the New York Bakery brand; frozen Parkerhouse style yeast and dinner rolls under the Sister Schubert's brand; salad dressings under the Marzetti, Cardini's, Marzetti Simply, and Girard's brands; vegetable and fruit dips under the Marzetti brand; Japanese barbecue sauces and dips under the Bachan's brand; and croutons and toppings under the New York Bakery, Chatham Village, and Marzetti brands. Its Foodservice segment sells custom-formulated sauces, salad dressings, frozen breads, yeast rolls, and frozen pasta under the Marzetti, Sister Schubert's, and Marzetti Frozen Pasta brands, as well as private labels for chain restaurants. The company sells its products through sales personnel, food brokers, and distributors to retailers and restaurants. The company was formerly known as Lancaster Colony Corporation and changed its name to The Marzetti Company in June 2025. The Marzetti Company was founded in 1896 and is based in Westerville, Ohio.

financial_summary: The Marzetti Company is a mid-cap consumer defensive business with a $2.9B market cap on $1.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 18% against a 7% cost of capital — a 12-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 24% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $206M in free cash flow — roughly 11 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.48× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.6× net debt/EBITDA.

Management returns a meaningful 5.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 29% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 1.5× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Input cost inflation from agricultural commodities — when raw materials spike, pass-through pricing lags and margin compression is immediate.
GLP-1 and health-trend demand destruction — weight-loss drugs and wellness shifts are structurally reducing consumption in snack, beverage, and packaged food categories.

sect: Its 12% operating margin runs 5pp above the Consumer Defensive median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 40% over the past year excluding the latest month.

The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 10%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $79.12 to $135 (P10-P90).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 44% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 7.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 5 covering analysts target $143 on average, 36% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.

prof: ROIC of 18% clears the cost of capital of 6.6% by 12pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.25).
It runs a 24% gross margin and converts 11% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.48x.
ROE of 18% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.5% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.6x net debt to EBITDA ($25.1M of cash against $199.3M of debt), with interest covered 135.4x.

growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.9% over 3 years, 5.6% over 5 years and 4.9% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 19.0% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 4.0% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 16, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has missed earnings estimates by 7.2% on average.
own: Insiders own 29.4%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 72%.
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 2 sales over the past year, net $136K sold.
It returns 5.1% a year to shareholders (1.3% in buybacks and 3.8% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 39 consecutive years, raising it 6.0% a year over the last five.
Short interest is elevated at 26.9% of the float, 4.6 days to cover.
people: With about 3,500 employees, each generates about $551K of revenue, in line with the Consumer Defensive median, and productivity has risen 3.9% a year.
That works out to $59K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.2M (4x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
